newsitem.title: BURMA: Burma tightens security to curb student unrest.
newsitem.headline: Burma tightens security to curb student unrest.

text.p: Burmese authorities set up more security checks in the tense capital on Tuesday to curb any fresh student unrest, as troubled city universities remained sealed and calm after there were no new overnight protests.
Witnesses said police and soldiers continued manning roadblocks in the vicinity of the Yangon Institute of Technology (YIT) and the Yangon University (YU).

All classes in the two campuses remained cancelled since Monday after hundreds of boarding students left for home indefinitely, fearing more unrest and that the government would close the universities.
Diplomatic sources said small groups of students were playing a hide-and-seek game with the authorities overnight and on Tuesday, turning up at various places in the capital and shouting slogans.
The diplomats also said monks in northern Mandalay had announced the formation of an "All Buddhist Monks Union" this week. Unions are illegal in Burma.
Witnesses said police had set up more roadblocks at some river bridges linking central and eastern Rangoon to check the identity papers of commuters.

The tense atmosphere also resulted in many parents choosing to keep their children away from high school and secondary schools in the area surrounding the sealed universities, fearing for their safety from possible unrest.
"I asked my son not to go to school today because of the situation. He should have an early Christmas holiday this year," a woman in her early 50s told Reuters.
Burma's tightly controlled state media have not reported the student protests over the past week.

In the last protests on Monday, about 120 YU students at a campus near the main one clashed with soldiers and police who stopped them from marching on the streets, apparently headed to the U.S. Embassy in Rangoon's central district.
Residents in the area said a few dozen students were rounded up by security forces carrying batons after they threw bricks and sticks at them.
Across town in eastern Rangoon, a number of students from Dagon University also held an anti-government rally on Monday evening. Their protest was also cut short by police and troops.
The latest student protests have been the worst seen in Rangoon since the student-led pro-democracy uprisings of 1988, which the military crushed leaving thousands dead or in jail.
The anti-government protests were triggered by charges of unfair police treatment of YIT students arrested after a brawl with restaurant owners in October.
Students also want the authorities to let them form student unions on campuses and are opposing moves to close the universities because of the latest unrest.

The ruling State Law and Order Restoration Council (SLORC) has linked opposition leader Aung San Suu Kyi's National League for Democracy (NLD) to the protests. The NLD has denied any ties with the students and deplored the government's use of violence in dealing with the students.

"We believe that long-term solutions to social and political problems can be found only through a process of negotiations and reconciliation," it said in a statement. "The NLD deplores the use of violence to put down the demonstrations.

"It has become an official practice to victimise the NLD whenever there are signs of public discontent," it added. "In addition to the arrests of NLD members, access to the house of NLD Secretary General Aung San Suu Kyi has been shut off and restriction has been placed upon her movement."
The SLORC said it had asked Suu Kyi to restrict her movements because of fears for her safety during this period of unrest. But she has protested against the request.
